subject: ChiShona
content: The ZIMSEC Grade 7 ChiShona exam has two papers. Paper 1 (7040/1, 1hr30) is 40 multiple-choice questions (A-D) covering 3 unseen comprehension passages (8-9 questions each) plus language items: tsumo, madimikira, nyaudzosingwi, fananidzo, mazita, zviito, synonyms/antonyms/homophones. Shade your chosen letter clearly in pencil; if you change your mind, erase fully before re-shading. Answer every question - there is no penalty for guessing. Paper 2 (7040/2, 1hr45) has two sections: Section A (20 marks) - choose ONE composition from five options (rondedzero/hurukuro/tsamba/mhan'arwa), write about 120 words. Section B (10 marks) - comprehension (5 marks, answer in full sentences) and summary/pfupiso (5 marks, about 35 words, one paragraph, no figurative language). Manage your time: roughly equal time per Paper 1 question (about 2 minutes each), and split Paper 2 time so composition gets slightly more than comprehension+summary combined. Always read all instructions before writing.

subject: ChiShona
content: Tsumo (proverbs) are short traditional sayings expressing deep wisdom about life, used historically for guidance, correction, and even settling disputes in traditional courts (dare). Exam question types: (1) complete a tsumo given its first half, (2) explain what a tsumo means, (3) match a tsumo to another with the same meaning, (4) match a tsumo to one with the opposite meaning. Study tip: group tsumo by theme - unity (e.g. 'Chara chimwe hachitswanyi inda' - one finger cannot crush a louse, meaning unity brings strength), consequences of actions ('Chinokanganwa idemo asi chigutsa hachikanganwi' - the axe forgets but the stump remembers, meaning the wrongdoer forgets but the victim remembers), reciprocity ('Kandiro kanoenda kunobva kamwe' - a plate that goes out returns with another, meaning kindness is repaid), and leadership/humility ('Gudo guru peta muswe kuti vaduku vagokwana' - the big baboon must fold its tail so the small ones can also fit, meaning leaders should be humble). When explaining meaning, always state both the literal picture AND the life lesson.

subject: ChiShona
content: Practice completing these (answers in brackets, meaning follows): 1. Chisi hachieri (chinoerwa) - a taboo does not respect itself, people must respect it. 2. Rume rimwe harikombi (churu) - one man cannot surround a termite mound, meaning teamwork is essential for big tasks. 3. Mwana asingachemi (anofira mumbereko) - a baby who doesn't cry dies on the back, meaning silence about a problem can be fatal; speak up. 4. Chakafukidza dzimba (matenga) - what covers houses is roofs, meaning every household has its private/hidden matters. 5. Ukama igasva (hunozadziswa nekudya) - kinship is a half-calabash, it's completed by sharing food/generosity. 6. Kunge zenze rakaputirwa mumakumbo (kunorema kutakura) - carrying something wrapped between the legs is heavy going, meaning some burdens are hard to bear alone. 7. Shiri inokwenya inoshura zvinodya (yakadzika mazai kure) - a bird that scratches is looking for food, but a wise one lays eggs far away for safety - meaning wisdom includes forward planning.

subject: ChiShona
content: Madimikira (idioms) are fixed figurative phrases whose overall meaning differs from the literal words, similar to English 'kick the bucket' meaning to die. Learn them grouped by emotion/theme: FEAR/SHOCK - 'kuona nyeredzi masikati' (to see stars in daytime = extreme pain/shock); ANGER - 'kutuka mhepo' (to curse the wind = to complain with no clear target, extreme frustration); WORRY - 'kudya moyo' (to eat one's heart = to worry deeply); HIDDEN DANGER - 'kupfuya nyoka mudumbu' (to raise a snake in one's stomach = secretly nursing a grudge or hidden enemy); STUBBORNNESS - 'kubvisa nzeve' (to remove one's ears = to refuse to listen to advice); DEATH/LOSS - 'kutsvedza parwizi' (to slip at the river = to suffer sudden misfortune). Exam tasks: explain meaning, complete an idiom, choose the idiom fitting a sentence blank, or find one with similar/opposite meaning. Tip: never use an idiom literally in your own writing unless it fits the emotional context perfectly.

subject: ChiShona
content: Nyaudzosingwi (ideophones) vividly dramatise sounds, actions or states, usually paired with 'kuti' (akati X). KEY SPELLING RULE: when reduplicated for emphasis, NO hyphen is used - write 'kota kota' not 'kota-kota'; 'piti piti' not 'piti-piti'. This is opposite to reduplicated adjectives, which DO take a hyphen (e.g. 'murefu-refu' for very tall). Common ideophones by category: STILLNESS/SHOCK - 'akati dzvi' (froze still), 'akati mwiro' (went silent in thought); SPEED - 'akati svo' (leapt quickly), 'akamhanya kunge tsuro' is actually a simile not ideophone - don't confuse the two; CONTINUOUS ACTION - 'mvura yakanaya yakati shwarara' (rained steadily); SUDDEN STOP/SILENCE - 'akati zii' (went completely quiet); FALLING/COLLAPSE - 'akadonha akati bvamu'. Exam format: complete a sentence by choosing the correct ideophone from 4 options, matched to the described action/sound.

subject: ChiShona
content: Zvimiso (punctuation marks) commonly tested: full stop (chiperengo/gwanza) ends a statement; question mark (chiziso) ends a question - remember questions like 'Unofara here?' need the mark even though they don't 'look' like English questions; comma (chifemo) separates items in a list of 3+ things (e.g. 'Ndakatenga tsvigiri, upfu, masamba, mazai nechingwa' - note comma before 'ne' is dropped, only used between other items); quotation marks (mawaya) enclose a person's exact spoken words in dialogue - and note that quoted speech should start with a capital letter inside the quotes. Common error: writing a direct-speech sentence without quotation marks around the spoken part, or without a comma separating the reporting clause from the quote. Practice: rewrite sentences inserting correct punctuation where it's missing, and identify which of several versions of a sentence is punctuated correctly.

subject: ChiShona
content: Frequent ChiShona spelling errors to watch for: (1) confusing similar consonant clusters that change word meaning entirely if mixed up; (2) wrongly joining words that must stay separate, or splitting words that must stay joined - e.g. certain compound time/place expressions are one word while others are two, and this must be memorised per word rather than guessed; (3) hyphenation confusion - reduplicated ADJECTIVES take a hyphen ('akasiyana-siyana' = various), but reduplicated IDEOPHONES do not ('piti piti'); (4) using foreign/slang words (chirungu chemumanjemanje) instead of accepted ChiShona equivalents in formal writing - e.g. avoid casual loanwords in a rondedzero; (5) getting capital letters wrong on proper nouns (names, days, months, places, titles of respect). Practice by proofreading sample sentences and spotting which one is spelled/joined correctly among 4 options - this exact question type appears in Paper 1.

subject: ChiShona
content: Fananidzo (similes) compare two things using 'kunge' or 'se-' (like/as). Structure: [subject] + [action/quality] + kunge/se + [comparison object]. Common examples by quality: SPEED - 'anomhanya kunge tsuro' (runs like a hare); FORGETFULNESS - 'ane hanganwa kunge gunguwo' (forgetful like a crow); WHITENESS/PURITY - 'chena kunge ruvhu'; STUBBORNNESS/TOUGHNESS - 'wakasimba kunge dombo'; SLIPPERINESS - 'kutedzera kunge chibage chakadira mafuta'. Exam tasks: (1) complete a simile given the first part, (2) identify which quality a simile is describing, (3) spot the incorrect/mismatched simile among 4 options - often the trap is swapping two similar animals known for different qualities (e.g. confusing a hare's speed with a tortoise's slowness). Tip: build a simple table of [animal/object -> quality it represents] to memorise quickly, since many similes recur across different exam papers.

subject: ChiShona
content: Zvirahwe (riddles) give a short descriptive clue about behaviour or appearance, and the listener must guess the hidden object/animal/idea. Traditionally shared in the evening for entertainment and to sharpen children's thinking. Exam format: a riddle-style clue is given, and learners choose the correct answer from 4 options. Practice riddles: (1) 'Kuenda humbangu, kudzoka humbangu' (goes one way, comes back the same way) - answer: motokari/mugwagwa (a vehicle on a road, or the road itself - context in the question determines which). (2) 'Rakazvirova rikazhamba' (it struck itself and roared) - answer: jongwe (a rooster, describing how it flaps its wings against itself before crowing). (3) 'Chinofamba chisina makumbo' - something that moves without legs - answer could be nyoka (snake) or mvura (water/river) depending on context given. Tip: read the FULL clue carefully since riddles often have more than one plausible answer - the exact wording narrows it to one correct option.

subject: ChiShona
topic: Zviito - Verb Tenses and Common Errors
content: Zviito (verbs) in ChiShona change form to show tense (when something happens) and this is a heavily tested accuracy area, especially in comprehension answers and compositions. Key tense markers: PAST (-aka-, -a-) e.g. 'ndakaenda' (I went); PRESENT CONTINUOUS (-ri ku-) e.g. 'ndiri kuenda' (I am going); FUTURE (-cha-) e.g. 'ndichaenda' (I will go); PAST HABITUAL/CONTINUOUS (-ai-) e.g. 'ndaienda' (I used to go). COMMON ERROR: mismatching a time-word with the wrong tense - e.g. saying 'nezuro ndiri kuenda' (yesterday I am going) is wrong; it must be 'nezuro ndakaenda' (yesterday I went). Similarly 'mangwana ndakaenda' is wrong; it must be 'mangwana ndichaenda' (tomorrow I will go). When writing a rondedzero about a past event, stay consistently in past tense throughout unless quoting direct speech. Practice: given a sentence with a time-word and a verb, decide if the tense matches correctly.

section: 8. Mazwi Anoreva Zvakasiyana, Zvakafanana uye Anopikisana
subject: ChiShona
content: This section covers three related word-relationship types. HOMOGRAPHS (mazwi anonyorwa zvakafanana asi achireva zvakasiyana) - same spelling, different meaning by context, e.g. a word for 'moon' also naming a calendar 'month'; a word for 'crying/tears' also naming a 'mourning ritual item'. Always read the full sentence to determine intended meaning. SYNONYMS (mazwi anoreva zvakafanana) - different words, same/similar meaning, e.g. words for 'quickly' that can substitute each other in a sentence without changing meaning. ANTONYMS (mazwi anopikisana) - opposite meanings, e.g. 'kukura' (to grow/be big) vs 'kudiki' (to be small); 'kutanga' (to start) vs 'kupedza' (to finish). Exam format for all three: given a word/sentence, choose the option that is a matching synonym, an opposite antonym, or the correct alternate meaning of a homograph used in context. Tip: practice by writing your own two sentences for a homograph to prove you understand both meanings.

subject: ChiShona
content: Mazita (nouns) in ChiShona are grouped into noun classes marked by prefixes, which affect how adjectives and verbs agree with them. Key classes learners should recognise at Grade 7 level: class 1/2 (people) mu-/va- e.g. muzukuru/vazukuru; class 3/4 (plants, some objects) mu-/mi- e.g. muti/miti (tree/trees); class 5/6 (paired/collective, often body parts, fruits) (ri)-/ma- e.g. zai/mazai (egg/eggs); class 7/8 (things, tools) chi-/zvi- e.g. chinhu/zvinhu (thing/things); class 9/10 (animals, borrowed words, often no visible prefix change) e.g. mbudzi/mbudzi (goat/goats - same form both numbers); class 11/10 lu-/dzi- less common at this level; class 15 (infinitives, verbal nouns) ku- e.g. kudya (eating/food). Exam tasks: identify the correct plural form of a noun, or identify which noun class a word belongs to based on its prefix pattern. Practice pairing singular-plural forms across different classes to build fluency.

subject: ChiShona
content: Ushoma (singular) and uzhinji (plural) forms follow the noun class prefix pattern (see Mazita section), but some nouns behave irregularly and must simply be memorised: class 9/10 nouns often look IDENTICAL in singular and plural (e.g. 'mbudzi' = one goat or many goats; 'shiri' = one bird or many birds) - the number is understood from context (a preceding number word, or the verb agreement) rather than the noun's own form. Borrowed/foreign-origin nouns often also keep one form for both numbers. Exam format: given a singular noun, supply its correct plural (or vice versa), including correctly changing the noun-class prefix (e.g. mwana -> vana; danga -> matanga; chikoro -> zvikoro). Common trap: learners wrongly add a plural prefix to nouns that already don't change (like animal names in class 9/10), so always check whether the noun's class actually changes form before answering.

subject: ChiShona
content: Shona kinship terms (ukama) are precise and frequently tested. Key terms: Babamukuru (father's older brother), Babamunini (father's younger brother), Sekuru (mother's brother, OR grandfather), Tete (father's sister), Mainini (mother's younger sister) / Maiguru (mother's older sister), Muzukuru (nephew/niece via sister's child, or grandchild), Mukuwasha (son-in-law, or man who married into the family), Muroora (daughter-in-law), Muramu (spouse's sibling, opposite sex to speaker), Tsano (spouse's sibling, same sex to speaker, informal joking relationship), Tezvara (father-in-law), Ambuya/Vamwene (mother-in-law, or grandmother), Tateguru (great-grandfather), Mbuya (grandmother). Marriage creates NEW relationship terms even for people not related by blood - e.g. a man's wife's sister's husband becomes his 'tsano'. Exam tasks describe a family scenario ('Munin'ina wababa ndi____') and ask for the correct term among 4 options. Build a family tree with these labels for the most effective revision.

subject: ChiShona
content: Mitupo (totems, often animals/body parts) identify Shona clan lineage; each pairs with zvidau (praise names) used to honour someone. Common pairs: Moyo (heart) - chidau: Chirandu; Shava (eland) - chidau: Mhofu/Museyamwa; Shumba (lion) - chidau: Murambwi/Nechigumira/Sipambi (varies by lineage); Nzou (elephant) - chidau: Samanyanga; Mbizi (zebra) - chidau: Marowa; Gumbo (leg) - chidau: Madyirapanze; Dziva (pool) - chidau associated with fishing/water clans; Tsivo (needle/awl) - associated with tailoring/craft clans; Dhliwayo is a praise name used within certain Moyo/Nzou related lineages depending on specific family history - exact pairings can vary slightly between families and regions, so exam answers should follow the most widely recognised pairing given in class. Exam format: given a totem, supply its praise name, or vice versa (fill-in-the-table style). Note totems also determine marriage taboos - people sharing the same totem are traditionally considered too closely related to marry.

section: 1-2. Rondedzero Yenhoroondo Netsanangudzo (Narrative and Descriptive Essays)
subject: ChiShona
topic: Writing a Narrative or Descriptive Essay
content: Rondedzero yenhoroondo (narrative essay) tells a story of events in time order - use a clear beginning (setting the scene), middle (the main events/conflict), and end (resolution/lesson learnt). Stay in one consistent tense (usually past) throughout except in quoted dialogue. Rondedzero yetsanangudzo (descriptive essay) describes a person, place or thing vividly using sensory detail (sight, sound, smell) and figurative language like fananidzo (similes) used APPROPRIATELY - don't force in a simile that doesn't fit. Target about 120 words for either type. Structure tip: plan 3-4 short paragraphs - opening/context, 1-2 body paragraphs with the core content, and a brief closing sentence. Common exam prompts: describing a memorable day, a frightening experience, a special place, or a person you admire. Always re-read your work and check tense consistency, spelling, and that you have not drifted off-topic.

subject: ChiShona
topic: Writing an Essay Based on a Proverb
content: A rondedzero yetsumo asks you to write a story or explanation that illustrates a given tsumo (proverb). Steps: (1) make sure you correctly understand the proverb's meaning before starting - misreading the proverb is the most costly error here; (2) invent or recall a short scenario/story where that lesson clearly plays out - e.g. for 'Chara chimwe hachitswanyi inda' (unity is strength), you might narrate how a group project failed until people cooperated; (3) make the connection between your story and the proverb's meaning clear, ideally referencing the proverb again near your conclusion; (4) keep to about 120 words with a clear narrative arc. Avoid simply defining the proverb without telling a story - examiners want to see the meaning demonstrated through action/plot, not just explained abstractly.

subject: ChiShona
content: A mhan'arwa is a formal report, often reporting an incident (theft, accident, damage) to an authority such as police or a school head. Essential structure: (1) heading/reference details - date, time, and place of the incident stated clearly near the start; (2) a clear statement of what happened, in time order; (3) specific details - who was involved, what was lost/damaged, how it was discovered; (4) any action already taken (e.g. informing a neighbour, calling for help); (5) a closing request or recommendation, such as asking for police to investigate. Keep the tone formal and factual - avoid emotional or exaggerated language, and avoid figurative expressions (proverbs, idioms) which don't suit a factual report. Target about 120 words. Common exam scenarios: reporting a break-in, a road accident witnessed, or storm damage to a building.

subject: ChiShona
content: A hurukuro is a written conversation between two or more named characters discussing a given topic (e.g. the importance of education, environmental conservation, respecting elders). Format: each speaker's name is written followed by a colon, then their words - e.g. 'Tawanda: Mhoroi shamwari.' Structure: (1) brief opening greeting/context-setting; (2) each speaker takes turns raising points relevant to the topic - alternate views or complementary ideas work well; (3) the conversation should show natural back-and-forth, not one-sided lecturing; (4) a closing exchange that wraps up the discussion, often with agreement or a shared resolution. Keep language natural and appropriate to the speakers (e.g. informal between friends, more respectful/formal between a child and an elder). Target about 120 words total across all speakers combined. Common error: forgetting the colon after each speaker's name, or having only one character actually contribute ideas.

section: 6-7. Rondedzero Yenhetembo Nemifananidzo (Poem and Picture-based Essays)
subject: ChiShona
topic: Writing from a Poem or Picture Prompt
content: Rondedzero yenhetembo asks you to write a composition inspired by or explaining a short poem's theme/message - read the poem carefully first, identify its central subject and mood, then build your composition around that. Rondedzero yemifananidzo (picture composition) asks you to write a story or description based on one or more images - examine every visible detail (people, setting, actions, expressions) and weave them into a coherent narrative rather than just listing what you see. For both types: (1) make sure your writing clearly connects to the given stimulus - don't drift into an unrelated topic; (2) use descriptive and narrative techniques together; (3) maintain the 120-word target and tense consistency; (4) if characters are shown/implied, you may invent plausible names and dialogue to enrich the piece, as long as it stays consistent with what's shown or described.

subject: ChiShona
topic: Writing a Discussion or Debate-style Essay
content: A rondedzero yenhaurwa presents and weighs different viewpoints on a topic (e.g. should children be given pocket money, is social media good or bad for youth). Structure: (1) brief introduction stating the topic; (2) present one side's viewpoint(s) with reasons; (3) present the opposing viewpoint(s) with reasons; (4) a concluding statement - this can either give your own balanced opinion or simply summarise both sides without necessarily choosing one, depending on how the question is phrased. Use connecting words to show contrast between viewpoints, such as words meaning 'however' or 'on the other hand', to make the structure clear to the reader. Avoid being purely one-sided if the prompt asks you to 'discuss' rather than 'argue for' one position - discussion implies showing balance. Keep to about 120 words, prioritising 2-3 solid points per side rather than many shallow ones.

subject: ChiShona
topic: Writing Tsamba - Friendly and Business Letters
content: Tsamba kuhama kana kushamwari (friendly/family letter): informal, warm tone; structure includes sender's address (top right), date, an affectionate greeting (e.g. 'Shamwari yangu inodiwa'), body paragraphs sharing news/feelings, a warm closing (e.g. 'Ndinokuda', 'Shamwari yako'), and signature. Tsamba yebasa (business/formal letter): formal tone throughout; structure includes sender's address, date, recipient's title/address, a formal salutation, a clear subject/reference line stating the letter's purpose, body paragraphs that are direct and factual, a formal closing (e.g. 'Ndinotenda', 'Muranda wenyu'), and full name/signature. Both letter types should stay around 120 words for the body. Common errors: mixing formal and informal tone within the same letter, forgetting the date or address, or failing to clearly state the letter's purpose early (especially in a tsamba yebasa, where the purpose should appear in the first paragraph, not buried later).

subject: ChiShona
content: General rules for answering ANY nzwisiso (comprehension) question, regardless of passage type: (1) read the whole passage 2-3 times before answering; (2) answer in FULL, grammatically complete sentences, never single words alone; (3) copy the question number exactly; (4) use the exact spelling of proper nouns/names as they appear in the passage; (5) do not answer using a proverb/idiom/figure of speech unless specifically asked to identify or explain one - default to plain, literal language; (6) when asked what a word 'means', explain it based on how it's used IN THAT SENTENCE of the passage, not a generic dictionary definition; (7) marks are awarded per point required, so if a question asks for 'two reasons', give exactly two clearly separated reasons, not one vague combined answer; (8) never introduce facts not stated or reasonably implied in the passage - stick strictly to what the text says.

section: B, C, E. Nzwisiso Yehurukuro, Tsamba (Dialogue and Letter Comprehension)
subject: ChiShona
content: When the comprehension passage is a hurukuro (dialogue), pay close attention to WHO says what - questions often ask you to identify which speaker made a particular statement or held a particular opinion, so track speaker names carefully as you read. Don't confuse one speaker's viewpoint with another's. When the passage is a tsamba (letter, friendly or business), note: the sender, the recipient, the date/place if given, and the main purpose of the letter stated early in its body - these details are frequently asked about directly. For both dialogue and letter comprehension, questions may also ask about tone (is the speaker/writer angry, happy, worried?) - base your answer on specific words or phrases in the text that signal that emotion, not on assumption. Always quote or closely paraphrase the relevant detail from the text to support your answer where the question calls for evidence.

subject: ChiShona
content: Poem comprehension (nzwisiso yenhetembo) tests understanding of theme, word meaning in poetic context, and figurative language. Approach: (1) read the poem twice - once for overall feeling/theme, once closely for detail; (2) identify the poem's main subject (e.g. praising a totem/clan, describing nature, teaching a moral) - this is often asked directly as 'what is this poem about?'; (3) when asked what a specific word or phrase means WITHIN the poem, consider the poetic/figurative sense, not just literal dictionary meaning, since poems often use symbolic or praise language (e.g. an animal name used as a praise term for a person's clan); (4) identify the poem's tone (praising, warning, mourning, celebrating); (5) if asked to identify the closing statement or final expression used by the poet, quote it as it appears. Poems in ChiShona exams are often clan praise poems (nhetembo dzemadzinza) - familiarity with common totem/praise vocabulary (see Mitupo Nezvidau notes) helps significantly here.

section: F, G. Nzwisiso Yegirafu Netafura (Graph and Table Comprehension)
subject: ChiShona
content: For girafu (graph) and tafura (table) comprehension, the passage is data rather than prose. Approach: (1) read the title/heading of the graph or table first to understand what it's showing overall; (2) check the axis labels (for graphs) or column/row headings (for tables) to understand the units being measured; (3) when asked to identify the highest, lowest, or a specific value, read the data point precisely rather than estimating; (4) when asked to compare two categories, state the comparison clearly in a full sentence, e.g. 'X yakawanda kupfuura Y' (X was more than Y); (5) when asked to calculate a difference or total, show your answer as a full sentence with the correct number word, not just a bare digit; (6) answers should still be written in complete ChiShona sentences even though the source material is numeric/visual, not prose.

subject: ChiShona
content: When the comprehension passage is a mhan'arwa (report/statement of an incident), focus on extracting factual details precisely: what happened, when, where, who was involved, and what outcome or action followed. Questions typically test whether you can locate a specific fact accurately (e.g. 'what time did the incident occur?', 'what was reported missing?') and whether you understand cause-and-effect relationships described in the report (e.g. what caused the damage, what action was recommended as a result). Since reports are factual and formal in tone, avoid embellishing your answers with opinion or figurative language - answer precisely with what the report states. If asked to summarise the report's main point in one sentence, focus on the core incident and its immediate consequence, leaving out minor supporting details.

subject: ChiShona
content: Pfupiso (summary, worth 5 marks) requires roughly 35 words in ONE continuous paragraph. Technique: (1) read the passage and the summary question carefully to identify exactly what aspect you must summarise (the question narrows the focus - e.g. 'summarise the steps taken to prevent X', not the whole passage); (2) underline or mentally note only the main ideas relevant to that specific focus, ignoring supporting examples/details; (3) rewrite those main ideas in YOUR OWN concise words, combined into flowing sentences - do not copy long phrases directly from the passage; (4) exclude all figurative language (tsumo, madimikira, nyaudzosingwi, fananidzo) - a summary must be plain and literal; (5) do not add your own opinions, feelings, or extra information not in the passage; (6) do not exceed the word limit substantially - going a little over is generally tolerated but padding the summary loses marks for lack of conciseness; (7) optionally note your word count at the end, e.g. '(Mazwi: Makumi matatu nemashanu)'.
